1. Introduction to Jurassic English™ Level 4
1.1
Mission
Statement:
Interpretive
Agency
and
Systemic
Critique
At Level 4: Mastery, the Jurassic English™ curriculum enters the realm of critical discourse analysis. Designed
for learners aged 12–14, Level 4 is engineered to cultivate Interpretive
Agency. At this stage, students no
longer assume the text is a neutral window into a story. Instead, they learn to read the narrator, interrogate the
structure, and deconstruct the language
of
manipulation. The mission is to transition students from consuming
literature to diagnosing it, treating English as a high-precision instrument for political, moral, and systemic
evaluation.
1.2
Pedagogical
Positioning:
Conquering
the
B2
Plateau
Level 4 attacks the notorious "B2 Plateau"—the most cognitively demanding stage in language development,
where progress often stalls. To move from B1 to B2, learners must master abstract concepts, subtext, irony,
and multi-perspectival analysis. We conquer this plateau not by drilling complex grammar, but by demanding
complex thought. By grappling with full novels, contested interpretations, and real-world stakes, the linguistic
sophistication (advanced conditionals, passive voice in academic writing, nuanced modals) emerges as a
necessary byproduct of the intellectual demand.

Statement
World Wise Learning (WWL) categorizes Level 4 as the crucial inﬂection point for media literacy and civic
readiness. In a digital age saturated with misinformation, the ability to recognize how vocabulary is weaponized
to short-circuit rational thought is a survival skill. This manual provides the blueprint for transforming the English
classroom into a laboratory for truth.

Lesson 13: Excavation — Visual Rhetoric and Linguistic
Deconstruction in Persepolis
Target

Grade
Level: Ages 12–14 years

Level: B1 →  B2 (Conquering the B2 Plateau)
Subject: English Language Arts (Jurassic English™ Level 4: Mastery)
Duration: 45 minutes
Overall
Learning
Goals
Students open the Persepolis dig site and expand the Excavation toolkit. Marjane Satrapi's graphic memoir
delivers argument through TWO simultaneous channels — words AND images. Today: deconstruct how the
panel composition, the high-contrast black-and-white inking, and the child-narrator's voice operate together as
a rhetorical mechanism. The text demands the reader analyze what the picture says that the caption cannot.
Teacher
Pre-Note:
This
is
the
ﬁrst
text
in
the
JE
library
that
uses
visual
rhetoric
as
a
primary
argumentation
channel.
Anchor
the
historical
context
BEFORE
opening
the
panel:
the
Iranian
Revolution
of
1979,
the
Shah's
fall,
the
establishment
of
the
Islamic
Republic,
the
mandatory
veil,
the
Iran-Iraq
War.
The
manual
is
explicit:
"Do
not
teach
the
text
without
its
historical/political
anchor."
Speciﬁc
Learning
Objectives
1. Students will independently regulate.
2. Students will deconstruct at least one panel using a Visual Rhetoric Decoder — analyzing composition,
contrast, framing, and the gap between image and caption.
3. Students will identify the rhetorical mechanism (Redeﬁnition, Appeal to Fear, or Circular Logic) operating in
the regime's language as Satrapi's child-narrator reports it.
4. Students will use B2 mechanism verbs (illustrates,
exposes,
dismantles,
manufactures) to articulate how the
dual visual-verbal channel functions.
Materials
Needed
Core Text: Persepolis by Marjane Satrapi (physical copies for all students).
One-page historical anchor handout: Iran 1979 — the Shah's fall, the Revolution, the Islamic Republic, the
veil decree, the Iran-Iraq War (1980–88).
Visual
Rhetoric
Decoder (4-column graphic organizer: Panel composition / Caption text / Gap between
image and caption / Rhetorical function).
Mechanism
Verbs
Reference
Card.
Highlighters.
Cool Down Passes.
